speechtext: That in accord with the recommendation contained in the report of the Select Committee on Standing Orders, the time for receiving petitions for Private Bills and also the time for presenting Private Bills be extended to Thursday, February 23rd, and Thursday, March 9th, respectively.	-

So as to elicit an expression of opinion from the right hon. the First Minister, I would point out that the rule providing that petitions for Private Bills shall be presented within a certain time was intended to facilitate the work of the session. If that time be too short, we should amend the rule and give a longer time, but the judgment of the House was that the time limit provided was sufficient. This rule, however, seems to be more honoured in the breach than in the observance, and last session I drew attention to that fact on several occasions. I pointed out that we might as well have no rule as one which we did not follow, and I think the House should either decide to amend the rule or insist on its being observed.
lit. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). It is quite true that my hon. friend from Grey has more than once called the attention of the House, and my own in particular, to the fact that the rule in question has been systematically violated. But I do not think that my hon. friend himself ever objected to this first request, which is invariably made, to have the rule extended. Since I have been in parliament it has been the constant practice to allow one extension at least ; but of late years this permission has been extended unduly, and last session we had the Committee on Standing Orders reporting in favour of an extension of time, not only once, but three or four times. But according to practice, this first extension is granted at once.
I do not object to this one.

The Conlmit-tee on Standing Orders should take notice, however, that the rule will not be extended any further. Of course, there may be exceptions, but if so, each application should stand on its own merits, and only be granted on special grounds. My hon. friend from Grey suggests that the rule should be amended. Perhaps we may have to revise, not only this, but several rules. For instance, we have a standing rule, which is never observed, fixing the recess for dinner from six to seven thirty p.m. By tacit consent, however, we have always extended that recess till eight o'clock. In the present instance, I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Grey agrees with me that there can be no objection to granting this extension, but that henceforth we should refuse all such applications.

I cannot quite agree with what has been said by either of the hon. gentlemen. Parliament is here to serve the people, and the people should have all reasonable accommodation in getting the legislation they desire. We are not here to tell the public, you must do this at such a time or you cannot have what you want ; but we ought to afford every reasonable facility to the public for getting the legislation they desire. There may be some very large interests desirous of obtaining legislation ; they may not be able to give the necessary notice, and I think we would be meeting the public convenience by receiving the Bills. I agree with the opinion that an explanation ought to be given, but I still think that it is a good doctrine that we ought to try and accommodate the public in so far as we can in giving them the legislation they may require ; we ought to accommodate them at least to that extent.

Certainly we ought to try and accommodate the public, but according to the British constitution, and i think also according to common sense, the public is better accommodated when there are rules surrounding that accommodation and which the public need to understand. But my hon. friend is a reformer, and perhaps he wants to accommodate the public without any rules at all. Perhaps he is in favour of some of those corporations who are generally suitors for private legislation.

The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) mistakes my point. The sessions are increasing in length, they are now four or five months long, and sometimes six months. There is no reason why these rules should not be liberalized-but, of course, the right hon. gentleman is always in favour of restriction.

The reason of the committee asking for this is this. The sec-ietary of the committee said that the Senate 15
had extended the time to February 23 to receive Petitions and one week longer to receive Bills and if we did not extend the time, all the petitions would go to the Standing Orders Committee of the Senate and none of them to the Commons committee, that is the reason why the committee unanimously recommended this to the House.

So much for the discussion on the present subject. But there was one remark dropped by my right hon. friend to which I wish to refer. He intimates that by common consent it has come to be the practice in this House not to assemble after recess until eight o'clock in the evening. If that is so, I am sorry that it is so. I think we lose half an hour of very valuable time. For my part I would much rather meet here at half past seven, which is according to the rules, and leave half an hour earlier, if either end is to be sacrificed. Last night we came here when very important estimates were up ; there was one minister ready to take his place and go on with his estimates. After a while another minister straggled in ; but for quite a while there was scarcely any gentlemen on the other side at all. I am sorry to say that our own side was sparse as well. But the government side is the side that ought to set a good example. I do not think it speaks well to the country when the important business of criticising and passing the estimates for the expenditure come up, that we should not on both sides show our own interest in the disposal of public business by being present. We were here last night, and it was a quarter past eight, or nearly so, before we got to work.
Oh, no.

It was after eight, and it seems to me we ought to get to work at half past seven. There is quite enough time [DOT] from six o'clock to half past seven to eat what should be ate at a meal for an ordinary man.

speechtext: BOLE (Winnipeg) moved to introduce a Bill (No. 23) to amend the provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada, 1902, with respect to common bawdy houses.
Explain.

My reason for introducing this Bill is owing to the fact that a decision of the courts of Manitoba holds that disorderly houses kept by one woman are not liable under the provisions of the Act. The amendment is intended to make houses of this character kept by one woman or more amenable to law and order. The necessity of this amendment is demonstrated in the city of Winnipeg, which I have the honour to represent. In that city disreputable houses conducted by one woman have been established oh some of our best streets, and the



good citizens have in some cases found it necessary to take the law in their own hands, by smashing windows and doors in their effort to suppress such nuisances.

speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if the government has any information to lay before the House as to the cause of the non-gazetting of the return of the member lately elected in the Yukon ? I understand that in the election in the Yukon, held on December 16 last, Dr. Thompson is said to be elected. The return has not yet been gazetted and the House, I believe, has no information as to whether any return has been made. I would suggest that, particularly at this time, when a Bill to provide for the autonomy of the Territories is about to be brought before parliament, it is important that the Yukon should be represented. It would seem that, if any person is to blame for the delay, the sooner that is discovered the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question of the return 15*
of the member elected for the Yukon came under the notice of the Secretary of State, who made inquiry as to the reason why the regular return had not been made. I desire to call the attention of the government to ap item appearing in the Montreal 'Daily Star ' in reference to the embargo on Canadian cattle. And, as this is a matter in which every hon. member is interested, and one that effects very deeply the interests of the country, I will take the liberty of reading a few lines. In the special cable correspondence dated February 1, is the following :-
Hon. Henry Chaplin, ex-Minister of Agriculture, started yesterday at Oakham a campaign in the rural constituencies against re-opening British ports to Canadian store cattle. He hotly denounced Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman for so trifling with the heavy responsibilities which may soon be his as a minister of the crown by favouring the re-exposure of British herds to the risk of disease after the enormous trouble and expense of stamping it

45(>
out. If the Canadian store cattle are readmitted, British agriculturists would again find their herds decimated by disease. The removal of the embargo would be an act of insanity, ruinous to the British cattle feeders.
And the correspondent sums it up under the head ' Canada's Problem.'
A most interesting political situation is thus created. The question asked is ' Can the Canadian government enable Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman to prove to parliament that the Canadian herds are absolutely free from risk of contagion from the American States ? '
I see by the press, particularly in the Toronto ' World,' the statement that the government is about to take active measures to secure the removal of the British embargo. I do not know whether that is a fact or not, but am quite aware that the government in common with members on this side of the House appreciate the importance of having that embargo removed. I submit that it is very important that the agitation now going on against the removal of the embargo should be, in some way, counteracted.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) if he suppressed any of the despatch he has just quoted from. We had the spectacle last year of that hon. gentleman reading a letter in the House and suppressing part of it.

I will, as a matter of privilege, reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpherson) at a suitable time. The public press, I hope, is open to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpherson), and I commend it to his consideration. The public press affords exceptional means of enlightenment, and I commend it to the hon. gentleman.
I would ask the hon. gentleman
Order.
I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) to hand the paper over to me, or to lay it on the table, so that I can see it for myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) has brought to the attention of the House a most important subject which is, apparently, to-day engaging the attention of public men in the old country. For some time past references have appeared in the British press and in the cable despatches in our own newspapers to the utterances of public men on both sides of politics on this subject in the political campaign now going on. I have watched closely the reports of these utterances.
I have felt, however, that it was not for any public men in Canada to interject into a political controversy in the old land-the view of the people of Canada upon this subject-I thought that it would injure the Mr. LENNOX.
position that Canada might occupy in the discussion of the subject with the British government when the time becomes ripe for re-opening the discussion. I may say, that, some time ago, the then Minister of Agriculture in England declared emphatically that there was no use in discussing that question, because the embargo would not be removed. That statement was called forth, I might say, by representations made by the government of Canada on this subject. We have felt, since an emphatic reply of that kind was given, that there was nothing further for us to do until an opportune occasion arose for re-opening the question. I may add that, within the last few weeks what appeared to me to be an opportune occasion for re-opening that question occurred. There was a report, apparently authentic, that the present Minister of Agriculture had declared publicly that, from his observation, the people of Canada seemed to be quite satisfied with the present condition of affairs, and that being the case there was no necessity for further discussing the matter. I took the liberty of immediately making a recommendation to His Excellency, that a despatch should be sent to the home government drawing attention to this utterance, asking if it were an official utterance, correctly reported, and pointing out that if it were, the Minister of Agriculture was labouring under a most grave misapprehension as to the condition of opinion on this question in Canada. So far no reply to that despatch has been received. The question is an important one in the interest of Canadian trade and in the interest of Canadian stock raisers and those who are in the live stock trade between Canada and the old land. I want to assure the hon. gentleman and the House that the question is one which is constantly watched on behalf of the government, and that every occasion that seems possible on which the views of the Canadian people and the interests of the Canadian trade can be furthered will be taken advantage of and has been taken advantage of.

I think it would be more within the comprehension of the House if the hon. minister would lay that despatch from which he has quoted on the table for the information of hon. members. No doubt we would all like to read that despatch. It is strong and eloquently expressed I have no doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will be very happy indeed to bring a copy of that despatch down at once.
Does the hon. Minister of Agriculture lay down the doctrine that it would be a good thing for Canadians to export their store cattle to England rather than fatten them here ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have never laid down any doctrine on that point, but I do lay down

the doctrine that it would be in the interest of the Canadian live stock trade to have the embargo removed.
Yes, but not for lean cattle.

As the bon. Minister of Agriculture effected a change in the United State regulations, perhaps he may be able to effect a change in the English regulations. The hon. minister took credit all over the country for having done that, claiming that he alone and not the American government had been all powerful.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I shall be very happy if I can do so.

speechtext:
For copies of correspondence exchanged between parties in the town of Verdun, county of Jacques Cartier, and the Montreal Harbour Board, or the Department of Marine and Fisheries, respecting protection against floods at Verdun, along the shore of the St. Lawrence River.
He said : Mr. Speaker, the object of this motion is to obtain copies of letters which have been addressed by parties in the town of Verdun near Montreal either to the harbour board of Montreal or to the government in regard to protection against floods. I may mention for the information of the House, that the town of Verdun has extended probably with greater rapidity and has developed faster than any other suburb of Montreal during the past eight years. In 1890 there were but a few houses where the town of Verdun stands to-day. The number of people residing there was so small that it was not then deemed necessary to hold a political meeting during the elections ol' 1890. To-day the town has a voters' list, I think, of over 1,000 names, there are four polling subdivisions, the population is large, the number of houses has increased in an extraordinary ratio, the street cars from Montreal pass through tfie town, has electric light, water and drainage and the place is increasing every day. Last year the town suffered a very serious reverse in the shape of an inundation caused by the rising of the St. Lawrence river during the spring freshets. The water inundated the town partly by coming into the tail race of the Montreal waterworks and overflowing the banks of the tail race. The bank is larger on the side of the city of Montreal than on the western side, that is on the side of Verdun, and the water poured in there in a single night in great quantities. It also came in in the ordinary way from the St. Lawrence river overflowing the banks of the river. I may mention that the damage was very considerable indeed. The protection afforded in the vicinity of Montreal against floods only extends into a part of
the town of Verdun, It would be necessary, to make that protection absolutely effective, to extend the wall higher up along the river St. Lawrence for some distance along the frontage of the town of Verdun. I saw by the papers that letters had been addressed to the harbour commissioners asking them to provide protection against a recurrence of such a disastrous accident as happened last year. I think it would be a very proper thing for my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Pre-fontaine), or the Department of Marine and Fisheries, to cause an investigation to be made by an engineer of the department, and I know of no engineer possibly who would be more competent to make that investigation than Mr. St. George who was for so long a time the engineer of the city of Montreal and who had occasion particularly to study this matter of inundations. I think it would be only justice to the people of Verdun if the hon. minister would cause an investigation to be made as to what would be the best protection to be afforded against inundations of the town from the St. Lawrence in that locality. As I read the statute, 57-58 Vic., chap. 48, which is the last Act having reference to the harbour commissioners of Montreal, it appears to me, that that part of the town of Verdun which requires protection is outside of the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners.
1	may be mistaken but I find in schedule
2	of the Act that I have just referred to that the western limit of the Montreal Harbour Board's jurisdiction is at the Little River St. Pierre and the inundation was caused by the situation of the land higher up than the entry of the Little River St. Pierre. If my interpretation of the schedule is correct it would be for the Department of Marine and Fisheries itself to look into the cause of that inundation and if possible to provide a remedy, because the results of last year's inundation were disastrous in the extreme. The damage was in a certain sense incalculable. These inundations, should they recur, would prevent the development of that thriving town, and if I am correctly informed by the people who know the locality well it would be very easy for the Department of Marine and Fisheries to provide adequate protection against inundation. I may mention, sir, that during the last election, the government candidate in the county of Jacques Cartier pledged himself solemnly as a supporter of the government that this matter would receive the immediate attention of the government.

Bill (No. 8) to amend the Mounted Police Act, 1894.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1, pay of the force.
How will this compare with the salaries now given ? [DOT]

At a previous stage I explained that the object of this Bill is to increase the pay of the officers by $400 and of the non-commissioned officer's and constables by 25 cents a day. At present, for instance, the commissioner who has charge of the police at Regina receives $2,600. He will receive $3,000. A superintendent receives if I remember rightly Mr. MONK.
$1,400 ; he will now receive $1,800. The inspectors receive $1,000 ; they will receive $1,400. I may say that this is the maximum, and it is not intended to give them that amount of increase at once. The plan we have adopted is that all officers who have been eight years in the service shall receive at once the increase of $400 ; all others will receive increases varying by $50 for each year that they have been in the service, until they reach $1,400. All those who have been eight years in the service will receive at once the increase of $400 ; those who have been seven years will receive an increase of $350 ; those who have been six years will receive $300 and those who have been one, year in the service will receive an increase of $50. The same principle applies to the constables.
How many assistant commissioners are there ?

The list of officers gives 55. Thirteen officers will at once receive the $400 ; two will receive $350 each ; two will receive $300 ; five will receive $250 ; eight will receive $200 ; two will receive $150 ; eight will receive $100 ; ten will receive $50 ; five will receive nothing.
Who is the commissioner ?
Colonel Perry.
What has become of his predecessor, Colonel Herchmer ?
He was superannuated in 1901 or 1902.
On how much ?
I cannot give the exact amount, whatever the law allows him. He came under the rules of the Civil Service and received just the amount that he was legally entitled to.
Before or after he went to South Africa ?
After his return.

This seems to be a somewhat large increase in salary all at once. To increase a man's salary from by $400 to $2,000 is an increase of 25 per cent. It seems to me there should be some good reason for such a large increase at one time. The Premier has not given us a reason for it.

I have on a previous occasion given the reason for if. Last year there was an expression of opinion on both sides of the House that the police were insufficiently paid, and my impression is that even with this increase in salaries the police will not be too highly

paid. Everything has gone up in price as my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) knows and in the west, where everything is growing very fast, the cost of living is far in excess of what it is in the east. For instance, the maximum pay of a superintendent is $100 less than that of a first-class clerk, and the maximum pay of an inspector is $100 less than that of a second-class clerk. Under these circumstances, I do not think the police are overpaid for the very important duties they perform, and in providing for them this very moderate increase I think we, are simply doing what the country would expect of us.

Notwithstanding that, I still contend that an explanation is necessary, and it seems to me that, coming from hon. gentlemen opposite, it is doubly necessary considering the doctrine they preached years ago when in opposition, that if they came to power they would make this a cheap country to live in. Now it is a dear country to live in, and the right hon. gentleman gives that as an excuse for these increases of salary. I am not complaining of the work done by the Mounted Police, because I think they do their work very well, and are entitled to as high pay as any similar class of men in the country. But it seems to me that when the increase is not a very moderate one, or is what some would regard as an immoderate one, some special reasons ought to be given for it. Last year we increased the salaries of the civil service in Ottawa, but I do not think that in any case the increase reached the proportion of the increase now proposed for the Mounted Police, an increase of 25 per cent at one jump.

I am afraid that the remarks of my hon. friend will make my modesty blush. It is true we said that we expected to make Canada a cheap country to live in, but we did not then anticipate that we would do as well as we have done, or that the country would be as prosperous as it is to-day, with immigrants going into the Northwest Territories at the rate of
150,000	a year. I am sure that my hon. friend will agree with me that the conditions are very different'from what they were in his time. I am surprised at the criticism of my hon. friend, and in future I shall have to resist the blandishments of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Last year they asked for increases of salary. I yielded to their demands, and now I am criticised. In spite of that, I think I shall have to persist in my good intention. For instance, Colonel Perry, the commissioner of the force, who receives $2,600, is to receive $3,000, which is certainly not an exaggerated price for the services he renders to the country. An inspector, who ranks, say, with a captain, receives to-day $1,000. There are men who have been in that class for twenty years or more, and they are to receive at once $1,400, while officers appointed last year will receive an increase only of $50, while those who have been inspectors for over a year will receive $1,100, and so on until they reach the maximum of $1,400. If my hon. friend will look at the facts as they are, and forget the speeches of former years, he will agree with me that these increases are very, reasonable.
I must say that for once I thoroughly agree with the right hon. gentleman.
Hear, hear- for once only.

I hope for more than once, but on this occasion at any rate. The Northwest is at the present time an exceedingly expensive country to live in. It is found by those who have business there that the salaries of almost every class of men have been raised, and the Mounted Police are certainly deserving of the most generous treatment that can be meted out to them.
What is the total number of the police now
Six hundred in the Northwest Territories and 300 in the Yukon.
Was there an increase of the force last year or the year before ?
There was an increase of 100 men last year.
How is the force distributed ?

There are about 85 posts distributed all over the Territories, from the American frontier to the mouth of the Mackenzie river and from the Red river to the Macleod district. We have established some new posts along the route of the Canadian Northern Railway, and we have two or three posts on the Mackenzie river between Slave lake and the mouth of the river.

Is the force generally being diminished in the eastern portion of the country, which is the more settled and the more rapidly increasing in population, and is the augmentation of the force in the parts farther west and north? My'right hon. friend knows that in earlier times, in the eastern parts of the Northwest Territories, the number of Mounted Police at the different stations was large, and they gradually came to do almost all the duties done by constables and police in the more settled districts. Before we went out of office we were gradually withdrawing the Mounted Police from the more thickly settled districts towards the east and sending them further north and west without augmenting the total number of the force. Is this process still going on, or is the force in the eastern districts still doing what the muni-

cipalities do down here, and what the municipalities will have to do up there as population flows in ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that we have made very little progress in that direction, and, if I remember aright, I do not think that the progress made by the government of my hon. friend in that direction was very marked either. We have experienced the same difficulty that was experienced by our predecessors. When we have made attempts to discontinue posts in a district that is sufficiently well settled to enable the people to take care of their own protection, we have received from all parts of the district the most unanimous protests against the removal of the force. AVe have demonstrated to the people again and again that they must take charge of their own police, especially now. when settlement is going northward, particularly into the Saskatchewan valley, where we have been obliged to establish new posts. But I must confess that I am not satisfied with the progress that we have been able to make in that direction.
AVill it be possible to reduce the force in the eastern portion of the Territories when the new provinces are created ?

Instead of reducing the force, we shall have to increase it. According as the Territories become more settled along the American frontier, there are greater opportunities afforded for stealing horses and cattle and smuggling and in other respects violating the law. We intend increasing the pay of the force by 25 cents a day. The pay of a colour sergeant, which to-day is $1.50 will be made $1.75. The pay of the other sergeants, which is $1, will be made $1.25. The pay of a corporal will be raised from 85 cents to $1.10 a day, and of a constable from 50 cents to 75 cents. We propose to raise the pay gradually. One-third will receive an increase of 25 cents and two-thirds an increase of from 10 to 20 cents.

So far as the increase of pay is concerned I do not feel disposed to raise any objection. AVe have a splendid body of men out there, and the country has been well repaid by the services of the force for the money it has cost. I do not expect that for years to come the total of the force will be diminished. It will, on the contrary, rather be increased, at any rate until municipal institutions are firmly established and tiie population becomes sufficiently large to keep up these institutions. I venture to express the hope that this force will be, as it was under the late government, kept entirely free from the blight of political partisanship and administered with a sole eye to merit.

What is meant by the term ' unorganized portions of the Northwest Territories ?' Is it that portion with-Mr. FOSTER.
out provincial autonomy or municipal organization ?

By that is meant the Mackenzie River territory and the forts very far north, also the Hudson Bay territory. AVe give the men there extra pay.
*
Does any portion of the Mounted Police operate in Manitoba ?
Yes, on the southern frontier.
How many men on Hudson Bay ?
A couple of years ago an officer and five men were sent there. I could not say how many are there now.

Is not the force at present the sole force charged with the maintenance of order in the territories not yet organized into provinces, and when that organization takes place will that not make a very considerable change in the duties of the force ! As soon as there is provincial organization there will be municipal institutions, and the duty of maintaining law and order will then devolve upon the local authorities ?

I must say at once that even after the territories are organized into provinces we do not see the feasibility of dispensing with the services of the force. Of course when the municipalities are organized they will have to look after their own protection, but there is still a very large Indian population in the country and a great many immigrants coming in, and we have to provide, not onB' against violations of the customs laws, but for the protection of lawr and order of every kind. I do not think I am slandering the neighbouring country when I say that there is a lawless element coming in from that country against which we have to guard constantly, and we are bound to take every precaution to show new settlers that in Canadian territory life and property are amply protected.
AVhen will the Bill for provincial organization he brought down ?
About the second week in February, but cannot say for certain.
The pay of the men is apart, I presume, from the rations ?
Yes, we provide rations beside the pay.

Of course, I do not want to annoy the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), but, remembering old days, I cannot but be impressed with the changes that time has brought in the opinions of hon. gentlemen opposite. I can remember, when hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side, when there was an urgent de-

mand from them for the reduction of the force, and reasons were strongly urged why the country should not be called upon to pay so much for a useless army. In fact, I believe, these urgings were so strong, that the government of that time did diminish the force by a couple of hundred men. But the right hon. prime minister and his friends later on, thought the force should be Increased again. I hope that increase was not made necessary by the kind of immigration the government is bringing into the Northwest. The government boasts loudly of increasing the immigration by hundreds of thousands ; but it is not difficult to effect that increase considering the quality of some of that immigration, and considering that the government spend annually $700,000 more than their predecessors in the promotion of immigration. I will not follow the example of the right hon. gentleman and his party when in opposition by finding fault with this measure. It is a good thing for the Northwest that we should have a good police force, and when these men render good service, they should be well paid.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is the usual item. It provides for the expense of general administration at Ottawa. There is no change except a statutory increase of $50 to the architect.
There is au architect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Formerly this officer was connected with the Kingston penitentiary. But I thought it better to remove him to headquarters. His salary is now charged against the general expenditure. He has been in the service for many years.
I suppose his work is in connection with repairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And construction-additional wings and that sort of thing.
Does the Department of Justice carry on construction of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. We get an appropriation for material, and use convict labour.
What is the staff at headquarters?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Two inspectors, the architect, officers contingencies and the expenses of the parole officer. That is a new officer appointed last year.
I suppose he looks after the paroled prisoners ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The man who is doing the work is not paid a salary but works voluntary. Mr. Archibald of the Salvation Army. He is doing an immense amount of good.
Will the minister explain what this officer does ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When a prisoner is about to be discharged upon parole, the officer is informed. He endeavours, as far as possible, to obtain employment for the man to help him in any way possible. If, for instance, the man is a mechanic, the officer provides him with a kit of tools. We have a vote of $2,000, part of which is placed at the disposal of the officer for these purposes.
What conclusion has the minister reached as to the results of this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My conclusion is indicated by the fact that I have asked Inspector Archibald to apply for his release from tlie head of the Salvation Army, so that he may be able to devote his whole time to this work at a fixed salary. Mr. Archibald is an eminently satisfactory official, and will be in a position to do good service in this branch of the administration.
Does the minister find it less difficult to get employment for the paroled men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is an institution in Toronto-I do not wish to mention the name openly-in which we have ten paroled men. We have received applications from employers who are ready to engage these men-of course, always on the recommendation of Mr. Archibald-and he takes the trouble to look after them after they leave the establishment. .
How many men were let out on parole last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) will look at page II the last report of the department he will find a comparative statement of the paroles, pardons, deaths and escapes. Last year, 122 men were paroled. We find the system to work most satisfactorily. One difficulty in connection with the parole is the reporting. The man paroled is obliged to report to the police officials of the locality in which he resides. I find that some of the police officials-and I make this statement here publicly in the hope that some good may come of it-are far too zealous. They go about and make trouble for the unfortunate paroled convict. I have a case in mind in which the convict himself told me that the police officers took the trouble to go to tlie employer and tell him that the man was

a paroled convict, and, in ways which I will not particularize succeeded in obliging the convict to leave his employment. That is an act of great cruelty, and I make mention of it that those who are guilty of such atrocious conduct may know that it does not receive the approval of parliament.
What is the proportion of the lapses ? You had 120 on parole but the year before would furnish a better figure to take.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The year before the number was 113. I do not know that I can find here the exact figures, but some time ago I asked the Commissioner of Dominion Police, Col. Sherwood, who has control of these discharged convicts so far as police supervision is concerned, and the report he made to me was that it would be about seven per cent. That I consider very satisfactory.
What is the principle upon which the hon. gentleman acts '!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the first place, the inspector visits the penitentiaries once or twice a year, when every convict in the penitentiary is entitled to see the inspector separate from the warden or any other officer, that is separate from Mr. Stewart and from Mr. Dawson. If the convict wishes to have his case brought before the minister, he makes his complaint to the inspector, who, on his return, makes a report to myself, and I take up the different cases and look into them. Or the convict may make a petition, or his friends on his behalf, to the department ; or another method is that he may apply" through Mr. Archibald, who goes about and visits all these penitentiaries, and who may make a request that a man be discharged on parole. Then the procedure is to apply to the convicting magistrate, or to the judge, for a report of his case.
On that one point-is it the practice of the department always to apply to the judge ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Invariably, it is a rule without exception. Of course it would be impossible properly" to deal with these cases if I did otherwise, I cannot have any knowledge of the facts brought out on the trial. I get the magistrate's report, then I apply to the warden in order to ascertain what the conduct of the convict has been while he was in the penitentiary". Then having before me the report of the committing magistrate, or judge, and the warden's report, I consider the case myself. If this has been a second offence, the application is almost without exception refused, except in a case where Mr. Archibald might point out some particular reason why under the circumstances the man should be paroled. But if it is a first offence, or if the convict is a young man and I see that he has an opportunity of getting employment, unless the Mr. FITZPATRICK.
convicting magistrate has reported strongly against him, so far as possible I help the man along. It may be that I have dealt somewhat generously with these people, but up to the present I have had no occasion to regret it. A first offender always receives consideration as far as it is possible to give it, especially if he is a young man. Then if he is allowed out he is obliged to report every month to the police officer in the locality where he resides.
Mr. FOSTER, This is different, of course, from a case where the minister, under the authority vested in him, pardons out an offender.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Is it the rule of the department in such cases always to get a report from the judge ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. There are two things that are essential in all cases whether the application is for pardon or for parole, that is to get a report of the trial from the judge and of the conditions under which sentence was given, and a report from the warden. That rule is never departed from.

There is a case I have in my mind which I must look into a little more before I bring it to the attention of the minister. The minister may understand that something like this takes place : There are men who seem particularly willing to take up the cases of men who are charged with crimes, and after having gone through the courts of law are sent down for punishment; there seems to be in some cases almost a mania with these individuals to take up a case like that and approach the minister or authorities and make capital, and perhaps money for themselves, by getting these persons pardoned out. Sometimes they succeed, not so much from the justice of the case, or the merits of the case involved, as from the fact that the person who is interesting himself has, as he thinks, large influence in the party, and he uses that influence for all it is worth in order to commend his case to the department. Now there are one or two cases which came before my own observation, and which, from the apparent circumstances, seemed to me to be rather gross. One of them I intend to talk over with my hon. friend, and if it is such as I think it is, I have no doubt that he will pay every consideration to what I may bring before him. I think it is a great mistake for criminals or others to get an idea into their heads that by getting certain influential persons to act as intermediaries in their behalf they can escape, to a certain extent, the penalty of the crimes they have committed. But the parole business is quite a different matter from that. I am glad to hear the minister say that in all cases it is his invariable rule, before either pardon or

parole is granted, to get the judgment of the court giving sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say in answer to my hon. friend that I have in my mind cases such as he refers to, and I can assure him that the gentlemen in question, probably the same person he refers to, has realized by this time that he has no access to the Do partment of Justice which any other person does not have. There is no royal road to the Department of Justice. I would like to add that there has never been a case decided by myself that had not previously been examined by Mr. Power, of the Department of Justice, a gentleman in whom we have the greatest possible confidence, who has had an experience extending over twenty years in dealing with matters of this kind. I can safely make this statement, that there is not a case in which I have taken action without a previous report by Mr. Power.

How frequent have reports to be made to the local authorities ?

The hon. minister states that on certain occasions he allows them to go to the United States. In that case does he require a report every month, and if so, to whom ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, if a man is permitted to go to the United States he is exempted from the obligation to report.
Every month ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. I am reminded of the condition under which the parole is granted. It is that they shall not leave the country.
If leave is given, and if they leave the country you do not expect a report from them ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Once a month. The convict is obliged to report each month to the local police authorities. If he fails to report, his case goes to the commissioner of police. If he does report, nothing is said, but if he fails to report each month, the commissioner of police is notified, and as a result applies to me for a cancellation of the ticket-of-leave, and the man goes back to the penitentiary.
Do I understand from the Minister of Justice that if a man fails to report he is recommitted to the penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the ruie.
What becomes of those who go to the United States, for example, beyond the jurisidiction of the minister ? How are they dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If a man goes to the United States without permission of the minister, he is dealt with as a man who has failed to report, and if he comes back he is iecommitted to the penitentiary. Very frequently it may happen that there is a condition attached to the pardon, and if a man violates that in going to the United States, and if his relatives bring him back then he would have to go back to the penitentiary and purge his sentence. But in the case of a paroled convict he may apply for leave to go to the United States, and it sometimes happens that I grant leave; in fact, I almost invariable grant it if a proper case is shown.

I would like to know how many at the present time are out on this ticket-of-leave. This is a question that considerable interest is taken in throughout the country, and any information the hon. minister can give I am sure will be appreciated.

Are there any cases of any persons who have been allowed out on ticket-of-leave being sent back to the penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh, yes-about seven per cent. I have not the exact figures here, but the inspector tells me that it is about seven per cent.
ill-. MONK. Last session two returns were ordered by the House. One was a return in respect to the parties allowed out on ticket-of-leave within a certain period of time. The other was a return as to the parties convicted of arson and who bad subsequently7 been allowed out on ticket-of-leave.
