speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at page II. of the report on penitentiaries, he will find the number of convicts who have been allowed out since the Act first came into force. In respect to the arson cases I have not the slightest recollection of what my hon. friend refers to. If he will be good enough to send me a note I will see that the information is brought down.

I understand from the hon. minister that seven per cent of those who have been allowed out have been returned to the penitentiary. May I ask whether they have been returned for failing to report or for some other criminal offence ? I desire to ascertain what effect this leniency of the minister has had upon criminals and upon the country generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If a man fails to report he is returned to the penitentiary unless cause is shown. I referred to a case a few minutes ago in which a man failed to report because he found that by reason of

his reporting he was hounded to death by the local police officials, and on a report to me by Inspector Archibald to that effect, I relieved him of obligation to report. If a man out on ticket-of-leave commits an offence which of itself would not require that he should be returned to the penitentiary, the simple fact that he has committed a breach of the law makes it necessary to send him back to the penitentiary to purge his original offence. For instance, if a man had three years further to serve, if I allowed him out on parole, if he committed an assault and he was brought before a magistrate and convicted of this offence for which he would probably have to serve a month he would have to go back to the penitentiary and purge his original sentence.

I understand that about seven per cent have been returned, some for failing to report and others for haying committed a breach of the peace whilst out on parole. What proportion has been returned for some criminal offence committed whilst out on parole ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly cannot give the information now, and I do not think that I have in my department the information to give that answer:- But, I will say that as a result of the Salvation Army- or perhaps I should not say that-but as a result of the work of Inspector Archibald, there is a great improvement in reference to the parole system, and I think if it should be possible for him to devote his whole time to this prison gate work, that the result will be that -we will have very few paroled men who will have to be treated as second offenders. Inspector Archibald is exceedingly sympathetic, he is exceedingly enthusiastic in the performance of this work, and I think the greatest possible good will result from his aid to the unfortunate whom we allow out on parole.

If the Salvation Army have accomplished so much, why should they not get the credit ? Why should you give it all to Inspector Archibald ? I think this is a recognition of the work they have accomplished which has done more for these unfortunate men than the machinery of the law, and in that case why not give them the credit ? It does seem to me that we should encourage the Salvation Army and try to further the work that they are now doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Originally the Salvation Army did prison gate work. When I became Minister of Justice it occurred to me that they were doing very good work and that they should be assisted. I entered into communication with Miss Eva Booth, then at the head of the Salvation Army, and as a result she suggested that Inspector Archibald should be specially charged with this work while maintaining his connection with the Salvation Army. But, she pointed Mr. FITZPATRICK.
cut that the Salvation Army as a body could not conduct this work to an extent beyond what they were doing. Inspector Archibald undertook to deal with the matter while remaining a member of the Salvation Army and the result is what I have explained. But, I think it necessary, and this is the suggestion of Inspector Archibald himself, that he should give his whole time to this work. There is quite enough for him to do if he gave his whole time to it, and he has applied to General Booth as an official of the Army for leave to engage in this work so that he may become a permanent official of the government.
Does the Salvation Army receive any assistance from the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
None whatever. We are simply paying the travelling expenses of Inspector Archibald, and there is $500 which we place at his disposal, and on which he can draw for'the purpose of procuring the ordinary necessaries that a convict may require to enable him to make a start in life again.
Mr. OtSLER. Inspector Archibald Is a member of the Salvation Army ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, he is the Inspector at Toronto.
The hon. minister will remember that there was a small appropriation taken last year for this purpose and !I would like to know how much has been spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amount appropriated last year was $1,500 for travelling expenses and $500 for assistance to paroled and discharged convicts-about $2,000 in all.
iMr. U. WILSON. I presume that the hon. minister is quite as well satisfied as he was a year ago with the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I am so well satisfied that I want to secure Inspector Archibald's services altogether for the department.

If I remember rightly.
I think that some of the convicts in the different penitentiaries do not wait until the law comes to their aid and they are released on parole. How many convicts escaped from the different penitentiaries last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those who took leave were one last year, one in 1902 and one in 1901. Of course, those who got away and were afterwards recaptured are not entered as escaped convicts.
My hon. friend speaks only of the one who never returned. Are the authorities still looking for him, or have you given up ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe we are still looking after him.
What was the last mews ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has not written me lately, hut I am not without hope that some information may be had of him.

This is a large item, and I would again urge, as I have urged for several session the putting- of the Auditor General's Report in the members' hands before the House meets. We have not yet got the whole report. I think it is most unfair to ask us to vote large sums like this without having been able to go through the details and to satisfy ourselves about them. This is in itself a strong argument for the printing of the Auditor General's Report in sections and its distribution to the members at their homes before they come here, because, as a rule, their time is fully occupied here with other matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know the rule of other departments, but if the hon. member looks at page 115 of my report he will find all the details of expenditure.
How long has that report been on the table ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think since Tuesday last, but the Auditor General's Report with respect to the Department of Justice has been on the table for at least a fortnight.
Does the ticket-of-leave system apply only to penitentiaries, or does it apply to those who are imprisoned in jails for terms of less than two years ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it does.

It is the same law ? I understood the minister to say that before interfering with the sentence he takes the opinion of the judge who has passed condemnation. In the case of Brunet, of Montreal, was there a report from the Chief Justice who condemned him ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Would my hon. friend bring down that report ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no need ; it was only about four lines. I never look for any report from the Chief Justice, beyond a statement to the effect that the jury passed on the facts, that he had passed sentence, and that that ended it so far as he was concerned.
So, in that case, the minister acted solely upon his own responsibility ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes ; I do not want to shift the burden ; I take it all on myself.
How many prisoners are there at present in the different penitentiaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at page 1 of the report he will find the prison population from 1894-5 down to last year. At the end of the last fiscal year the prison population was 1,286. At the present time it is 1,400.
In all the peniten-ti'aa-ies ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any way of determining, from the increase or decrease of population, whether there is an increase or decrease in the morality of the country, if I may call it that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the prison population is any index to the morality of the country, I would say that the morality is almost stationary. For instance, in 1894-5 the prison population was 1,250 : in 1897-8 it was 1.415 ; last year it was 1,286, and at the present moment it is 1,400. So you see it does not vary greatly.

Is there no way of reducing the expense to the country of the maintenance of prisoners ? I have not made a special study of the matter, but I have read something about it, and in some countries they utilize the services of these men. All of us who have had dealings with the criminal courts know that many of these men are in the habit'of living in penitentiaries. Some of them do not conceal the fact that thpy live better in the penitentiaries than at home ; they cost on an average about $300 a year. Could their services not be profitably employed, for instance, in the macadamizing of roads ? There was a discussion on the employment of prisoners some years ago, but some opposition was made to it by some of the workingmen's societies on the ground that it would encroach on their own revenues ; but if they were employed on such work as the macadamizing of roads, which is not now done, they would not interfere with the labour market. Any one who knows our province knows that the roads are in a dreadful condition, and my impression is that if these men were engaged in outdoor work from 7 in the morning until 6 at night, like ordinary workingmen, they would not be in the penitentiary so often. I am only throwing out a suggestion, and I think this plan would be in the interests of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One of the difficult problems connected with the administration of justice is to find useful employment for the criminals, not only for the advantage to. be derived from their labour, but for the benefit to themselves from being employed. There is not a penitentiary which has not some industry connected with it. At St. Vincent de Paul we have a very large farm, in connection with which we employ a great many convicts. In addition to that, there is a great deal of stone cutting, and, until

(recently, quite large building operations were carried on, while a certain number of men are employed in the tailor and shoe shops. That is to say, we endeavour, as far as possible, to utilize the services of the convicts for the purpose of doing all the work required in the penitentiary. At Kingston we endeavour to run, with more or less profit and success, a binder twine industry, and as far as possible, speaking generally, throughout the whole country we utilize the services of convicts. We realize what my hon. friend says, that it is necessary to keep these gentlemen busy.

I understand that the work they do is done for themselves, such as the making of their own boots and clothing ; but, of course, a good deal of money is required to purchase the raw materials. I do not think this goes far enough in the direction I indicated. I would like the convicts to do outside work that would not interfere with the employment of other people, such as road-making. I mention this as one of the things that might be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have often thought of the possibility of utilizing these men, as on the continent, in connection with roadmaking. We have control of the convicts so long as they are within the penitentiary grounds, but not beyond the boundary of the penitentiary. The' benefit of their work would result to the municipality in which the penitentiary is situated. We could not take the convicts to a distance, because we would have to provide for them.
It would not cost more than it does at the present time. The men could be taken to any part of the province at a cost of not more than $300 a year each, and it costs that much to keep them now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We know what it is to take criminals about. We have some-[DOT] times to bring men from Manitoba to St. Vincent de Paul because there is not room for them in the Manitoba penitentiary, and it costs an enormous amount of money. My hon. friend would be shocked if I told him the number of guards that we have to send with these men.

It is done elsewhere. The cqnvicts who are put to work on the farm or breaking stone are the ones that have nearly finished their term. They are looked on as the safest to be trusted, although two of those who last escaped were among these. There are guards to look after these men, and the only extra expense to which the country would be put would be for feeding the guards. The prisoners have to be fed now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where would you house them?

This work is done during the summer. An army of thousands Mr. FITZPATRICK.
of men can be provided for while engaged in making roads. They could camp.
Mr. FITZPATRICK Pic-nicing.

I am serious about this matter. We are paying an enormous amount of money for the maintenance of men whom we do not redeem. My opinion is that any man who has been in the penitentiary for a few years cannot do any good. Some time ago a man came to my office looking for work. He had formerly been in good circumstances, but had been in the penitentiary for eight or ten years. AVhile there he had learned the trade of a painter, and he told me that although he had been out of the country, people knew that he had been a convict, and he could not get work anywhere.

In looking through the items given for Kingston, St. Vincent de Paul. Dorchester, Manitoba and elsewhere, and comparing them with the items in the Auditor General's Report, I find, roughly speaking, that about half the amount proposed to be voted for each of these penitentiaries can be classified under miscellaneous expenses, which are made up almost entirely of purchases of various articles, I presume, needed for the penitentiary. I would like to ask the minister what system is employed in the purchasing of these articles-whether tenders are called for. by whom they are purchased, whether instructions are given that they should be purchased in certain localities, and whether those who make the purchases are absolutely free to buy in the cheapest market.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The practice followed is that which has been in vogue ever since the penitentiaries were established. We call for tenders for everything.
Are the tenders called for by public advertisement or only from a few persons?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By public advertisement. If my hon. friend will look at the newspapers for the month of June, he will see the advertisement calling for tenders for supplies for the penitentiaries.
Are there not a lot of articles which are purchased otherwise than by public tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think everything that can possibly be supplied is bought by public tender.
What does the advertisement cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Dry goods, groceries, coal, meat, bread, hardware, lumber, building material, leather-everything you can possibly expect to get in a penitentiary.
And the contract always given to the lowest tenderer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All I know is that the inspectors make a report to me and I approve of it. I do not think my hon. friend can point to a case where the lowest tender has not been accepted. I think there was one case where we were purchasing a superior quality of cloth. Our inspector says the rule is never departed from, that the lowest tender Is always accepted.
I understood that St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary was lighted by electricity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is now.
Do I understand that the whole village is also lighted by electricity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We light the penitentiary and the street on which the penitentiary is situated, and which leads down to the station. That is for our own protection.
Mr. BERGERON! No other street?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No other street.
Are there not private citizens who are using the electric light and paying the government for it? I am not criticising, but merely asking for information?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. The convent near by and some private persons asked if we would not supply electrictiy, but we thought it would be inconvenient to do so, and we did not entertain the application.
Kingston Penitentiary, $177,600.
I find here an item of $62,400 for salaries and retiring allowances. Will the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the left hand column of my report, at the top of page 115, my hon. friend will see that the total foi the warden, Protestant chaplain, Roman Catholic chaplain, accountant, engineer, &c., is $61,355.02.
Was there an officer retired during the year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, a keeper, named Weir, who became physically incapable of performing his duties.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to certain items in the Auditor General's Report, page M-21. Beardmore & Co., Toronto, leather, $1,024; The Canadian Locomotive Co., of Kingston, $1,408 ; Garneau & Son, Quebec, dry goods, $1,980 ; M. McLaughlin & Co., Toronto, flour, $4,585 ; Rathbun & Co., cement, $652 ; Swift & Co., Kingston, hard coal, $2,691; Were all these items tendered for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those supplied by Beardmore, Garneau and McLaughlin certainly were, because they are staple articles. The Kingston Locomotive Works supplied the castings used in connection with the new wing. There was no public tender asked for in that case but tenders were asked for by circular.
Would not that be applicable to the Beardmore Co.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, public tenders were asked for in the case of the leather, dry goods and flour supplies.

The Beardmore people and the Canadian Locomotive Co., are well known as pretty strong Liberals. The latter is the company in which the hon, member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) is interested. Probably that accounts for their getting the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is not quite fair. The Ogilvies are supplying flour for the current year.

Take the case of the George Plunkett contract for coal. Kingston if, very much nearer the American side, yet Geo. Plunkett of Cobourg, whose politics arc very pronounced, got the contract. Were tenders called for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, by public advertisement.
Who else tendered fof it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There were a great number of tenders for the coal. I am glad to hear my hon. friend criticise me for giving contracts to Liberals, because I have had a great deal of criticism for doing the reverse from other quarters. The McLaughlin Company has been represented to me as very strongly Conservative.

I would like to come to the assistance of the hon. minister with regard to the coal in Montreal. All the coal there was ordered from T. F. Moore & Co., and there can be no danger of any reproach from the other side with regard to that firm. I presume that coal is tendered for by everybody at the same price ? In Montreal the important bodies, such as the municipal and school boards, generally divide their orders among the coal dealers. I think my hon. friend next year, even at the risk of getting reproaches from his own side, '*might follow that plan and not give the whole order to Moore & Co.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Those bodies to which my hon. friend refers have greater latitude than I have. They have not got a critical opposition to take care of them. (If we were to distribute the coal orders around among the different firms, we would be charged with not getting the lowest price.
Mr. (MONK. It is all the same price.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, if it were, 1 might take care of some people that I cannot now. There was a firm which grievously complained that I could not give them any part of the coal contract ; hut the reason was their prices were not low enough.

Were all the goods purchased from Hamilton Bros., who received a contract to the extent of $1,330, last year for the Kingston penitentiary and $1,670 for St. Vincent de Paul, the result of tenders.
' Mr. FITZPATRICK. Yes.
What methods are used to know that the goods delivered are according to sample ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have a storekeeper at St. Vincent de Paul, who has been there many years. He weighs and measures the goods, and I have never heard any complaint as to his work not being done properly.
Has he any samples or standards or descriptions which will enable him to make sure that the goods delivered are according to order ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the tenders are asked for, he has the samples and compares the goods delivered with the samples.
Was the same process followed in the case of Lewis Bros., of Montreal, who figure very largely ? They supplied Kingston penitentiary with goods to the extent of $1,892 and St. Vincent de Paul $1,123.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These goods were all purchased after tenders were called.
Will the hon. minister lay on the table the forms of tenders used ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the slightest objection, they have grown sacred by long usage.
How many tenders were received for the coal supplied by Geo. Plunkett, of Cobourg ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot tell the number now but I know there were several.
When are the tenders received?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In June.
Can the minister tell whether the coal was delivered from Cobourg?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The teuders required that the coal intended'for St. Vincent de Paul should be delivered at St. Vincent de Paul and that for Kingston at the wharf at Kingston.
Mr. BENNETT I am informed that Mr. Plunkett is not a coal merchant altogether, Mr. MONK.
but a hotelkeeper. We had a case of this kind yesterday, a publican-not necessarily a sinner-dealing in government supplies. I am informed also that Mr. Plunkett is not a dealer in a large way. Will the minister, when his estimates are next taken up, bring the tenders that were received? The amount involved is about $15,000-a considerable sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will bring the tenders.
Will the minister describe how the tenders are received and opened and the contract awarded?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is information called for to-day that has not been asked for in the last eight years.
This is a new House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Evidently-a very
new House, in some respects. So far, as 1 know, tenders are advertised for in the newspapers. They are received by the inspectors and opened by them. A tabulated statement of the tenders is prepared and 1 sign the order to award the contract to the person recommended by the inspectors.

I may say for the minister's information that attention was publicly directed to a number of these names figuring in the Kingston penitentiary accounts on the occasion of the recent Liberal convention in Toronto. I do not like to refer unkindly to the deceased-and I suppose we may say that the Ontario Liberal government is deceased-but during that convention, it was asserted in at least one newspaper that certain persons prominent in that convention -were interested in the supplies for Kingston penitentiary, and that this would account for their enthusiasm' at the convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman specify ? I do not think that Gar-neau was there or Lewis Brothers.
These were not connected with Kingston. I remember that there was a long list in the newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman bring the newspapers when I bring the tenders.

I will.
Penitentiaries-St. Vincent de Paul, $99,750

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is an increase of $400 there. It is to supply another pair of horses. It appears that the horses there have reached the age, one of eighteen years and the other twenty-one years, and it is about time we got rid of them.
Penitentiaries-Dorchester, $59,700.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no increase there.
Who is the warden?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. J. A. Kirk.
At one time in parliament. Mr. FITZPATRICK. I never saw him. Penitentiaries-Manitoba, $59,800.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are several increases in this vote owing to the increase in population. W'e are obliged to have three more permanent guards at $600 a year, and one temporary guard at $500. There is an increase also in the maintenance of convicts, due to increase in the number. The population of the penitentiary is to-day 188-it has gone up even in the last few days-against 140 on June 30, 1903. The item of industries shows an increase, which is due to the fact that we need wood for burning brick to be used in building operations. There is an increase under the item of lands and buildings, because we are obliged to construct an additional wing for which we require material which will cost $3,500.
Penitentiaries-Ifegina Jail, $12,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is an increase of salaries to provide for the employment of a temporary turnkey from time to time as required. Maintenance of prisoners [DOT]and discharge expense is increased because the population is now forty-two, as against an average for last year of twenty-seven. There is an increase on account of industries because additional farm implements must be purchased.
Penitentiaries-Prince Albert Jail, $8,650.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is an increase in salaries because, owing to increase of population, an additional turnkey must be employed at $600 a year. I have decided to increase the jailer's salary by $100. He threatened to leave because the salary was too small. The population now is twenty-seven against a daily average for 1903-4 of fourteen. There is a. slight increase in the cost of uniforms, owing to the additional officer, and in maintenance of prisoners and the discharge expenses because of the increase of population.
Penitentiaries-Edmonton Jail, $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a new institution. The expectation is that the building will be ready for occupation in July or August. It will have twenty-five cells for convicted males, seven for males awaiting trial, seven for females, and three for insane-a total of forty-two. This will provide, accommodation for prisoners from Alberta. At present there are twelve prisoners from Alberta in the jails at Regina and Prince Albert, and fifty-two more in the Northwest Mounted Police guardrooms. I expect this Edmonton jail will be the penitentiary for the new provinces when they are established.
One of the new provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One of the new provinces or the new province.
What is the system of purchasing supplies for the binder twine industry at Kingston?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Two dealers in the hemp market in New York furnish quotations and the material is bought from New York, and sometimes from England.
Who makes the purchases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The penitentiary officials send the prices here and receive authority to make the purchases, and they make them direct.
What was the result of that industry last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will find the details at page 5 appendix A of the report of the Department of Justice.
1. Twine manufactured :-The following is a summary of twine manufactured :
Pure manilla, 600 feet	415,925	lbs.Mixed manilla, 550 feet	125,490	"Rope yarn	
58,850	"
600,265 "
On the next page he will find the quantity sold.
How does it work out as regards receipts and expenditures ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a difference of opinion about that. The inspector considers that it works out satisfactorily in this respect, that receipts and expenditures about balance. We allow 30 cents a day for convict labour. It is about as much as the labour is worth, because they are not very expert nor desirous to learn.
How do you make the sales ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Sales are made to farmers only. Since July 1, 1901, farmers may send in club orders, and the order must be signed by the farmers who use the twine, stating the kind of twine and the quantity they require. The price is fixed by the inspector, who takes into account the amount that he has been obliged to expend to produce the article, and at the same time he pays some attention to the price in the market. But they generally grade their price a little below the market price, about a cent or a fraction of a cent below it.
We were told last year that they sold it at cost price.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a little below the market price. Where you have convict labour of this sort and allow anything at all for the labour, it is almost impossible to tell what the real cost to the government



is. There is also interest to be taken into [DOT]account, and the wear and tear of machinery.

I understood that was all figured out, and that convict labour was reckoned at fifty cents a day. Could the minister tell us how much they sold last year to farmers, and if any twine was sold to any other parties but farmers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not a pound to any one but farmers.
Was the whole output sold ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, during 1903-4 we sold 401,557 pounds. We had on hand June 30, 1904, 522,680 pounds. Since July 1 we have sold 209,705 pounds.
That makes 600,000 pounds that you have sold. How much did you make last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The total quantity offered for sale in 1903-4 was 924,237 pounds. Quantity manufactured in 1903-4, 541,415 pounds. So long as we have to observe the rule laid down by the House of selling to farmers only, we will have this result every year. We have now 382,822 pounds on hand, but there is an order of the House that we must sell to farmers at the price fixed. The proper way to do would be to dispose of it by public auction.
Is there any particular time when the orders have to be in from tiie farmers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, we sell to farmers at any time.

There is an impression amongst the farmers in our section of the country, that unless the orders are in at a certain time they cannot be supplied ; and that time is so early in the season that the farmers are not in a position to advance the money a month or two before they want the twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Orders may come in at any time.
The notices given in the newspapers would not bear out that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My information is that the difficulty my hon. friend refers to is caused by the fact that about two years ago we had only a certain limited quantity of 650-feet-to-the-pound twine, and that one class was exhausted, and when orders for lit came in the applicants had to take the ordinary run of twine.

I think the whole twine business has this defect. Last year or the year before the surplus on hand was sold to a private party at five cents a pound, while in round figures you are asking ten cents a pound from the farmers. Now twine was offered at about the same price as you could Mr. FITZPATRICK.
get it' in any country store. There was surely no inducement for farmers to send for it if they could buy it at a hardware store as they required it and used it up, they would prefer to do that than to send to the penitentiary for it weeks before they needed it. They would naturally go to the most convenient place to get it. But it is believed, and I think there were grounds for the belief, that the twine was not sold to the farmers at cost price. Add the one cent per pound, or the fraction of a cent that is added to cover any loss, to the price of the raw material, and the way it was turned out by others-all that left the impression, though the government states that they sold twine just a little below what others were selling it at, that in fact they sold it at about the same price. We were informed also from other sources that it was not the intention of the government to become competitors with others who were in that business, or to sell below them, because if they did they were destroying their market.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Whjit my hon. friend says illustrates the difficulty we have in dealing with this business. We have a mill that produces 400 tons. I understand that is only a very small fraction of the total quantity required in Canada. Now we cannot attempt to regulate the market with such an output as that.
But you can sell the twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Can the hon. minister tell me what kind of twine is that which he has on hand ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I think you are manufacturing a class of twine that the farmers do not use as extensively as they used to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My figures only go to June 30 : Pure manilla, 600 feet to the pound; mixed manilla, 500 feet to the pound.

The hon. minister has an inspector of binder twine, and that gentleman ought to know the kind of twine that is mostly used by farmers. He should get that information, and the penitentiary should make the kind of twine that the farmers use now. One class of twine that was formerly used, the farmers do not find it expedient to use now, and if that gentleman would have the class of twine made in the penitentiary that is generally used in the Dominion, the hon. minister would not find so much op hand.
Mr. FITZPATRICK, Thai; gentleman] does report, and the inspector tells me that we act on his report.
Does he report upon that line ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. This whole business of manufacturing binder twine is a charge oh the public. In my mind, there is no doubt about that.
How many men do you employ ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Forty convicts out of a present population of 448.
You do not give employment to 10 per cent of the prisoners.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not 10 per cent.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if the farmers know that this twine is to be purchased there ? I venture to say that there is not one-quarter of our farmers who know that they can purchase twine any cheaper there than they can anywhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will take up the report of the Minister of Justice, and look at page 0, he will see the form of circular that is sent out all over the country, in addition to which there is an advertisement published in the newspapers.
Which papers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot give the list.

I am not talking from a political point of view. These advertisements should be published in the small papers. There are a great many people who 16i
do not take the papers from Toronto, but who require binder twine. If the local papers had a chance to publish this advertisement it would produce better results.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that weekly local papers are chiefly used for this purpose.
In Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he can give us the factory cost of these twines ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The figures I gave a moment ago as representing the price at which these twines are sold, are supposed to represent practically the cost of production, but I imagine that if you take into account the initial cost of the plaut, the loss at which it had been run for several years, depreciation and one thing and another, you would find that we are paying a great deal more than we are charging for our twine. However, that is not the opinion of our officials. Here is what is represented to be the cost of the fibre for two years : Manilla fibre, January, 1903, $8.75 per cwt.; 1904, $9.25 per cwt.; average cost, 1903, $8.70 per cwt.; 1904, $9.50 ; sisal, average cost, 1903, $7.77 ; 1904, $7.45.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if there were not quite a number of complaints from the farmers who got this twine last season about the inferiority of it ?	i

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not last season. There were complaints before, but not last season. We will occasionally have a complaint or two from people who do not want to pay their debts, but we have had three hundred letters from farmers in different parts of the country commending the twine.

I do not wish to get into a discussion as to whether the parties who made these complaints were able to pay their debts or not, because I know that the people with whom I was speaking were perfectly willing and able to pay their bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where were the complaints from-Prince Edward Island ?
Yes. They usually pay their bills down there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And they send men up here who do that.

We always try to do that, too. There were really some serious complaints from some of our most reputable farmers, who said that the twine knotted and broke, and they have made complaints directly to the department about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is my hon. friend quite sure that these complaints were made in respect to the twine sold during last season ?	,
I understand so. People claimed to have a great deal of twine which they tried to use, but which they finally had to abandon and were compelled to buy other twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The inspector, who is more familiar with the details of this matter than I am, says he has no recollection of any complaint during last season from Prince Edward Island. We did have a few complaints from Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, but none from Prince Edward Island.
I will recall the name to the hon. minister of one of the parties to whom I refer. Mr. Lee, of Victoria, sent in one complaint.

The fact remains that the sale of binder twine direct to the farmer has been a decided success. My hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) shakes his head at that, but the facts bear out my statement. We find by the record that a few years ago twine was sold to supporters of the government without any tender at a very low price, and the complaint that was made in the House was that the farmers did not have an opportunity of purchasing the twine. Taking up the Auditor General's Report for this year, I find that since the new resolution was adopted by the House almost 500 farmers in Canada ordered direct from the penitentiary and secured then- twine. I pointed out last year and the year before that in my humble opinion the penitentiary was manufacturing too many kinds of twine, that what the farmers want is pure manilla twine. That is about the only kind that is sold generally, in Ontario, at leask.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We manufacture manilla and mixed manilla.

Mixed is not a pure manilla twine. It is sisal and manilla mixed. The farmers do not wish to use that kind of twine. The demand is for a pure manilla twine, and if the Kingston penitentiary were to manufacture a pure manilla twine and put it on the market at cost, or a little over cost, it is useless for any man to stand up in this House and say that the farmers would not purchase it. My hon. friend has already stated that the amount of twine manufactured at the Kingston penitentiary is very small in comparison with the consumption. I would like to ask the hon. minister what [DOT] amount of twine remains unsold at the penitentiary at this moment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On June 30, 1904, we had on hand:-
Pure manilla, 600 feet to the pound, 320,085 lbs.
Mixed manilla, 550 feet to the pound, 120,900 lbs.
Of that we have sold since that date:- Mr. FITZPATRICK.
Of pure manilla, 189,400 lbs.
Of mixed manilla, 17,745 lbs.
My information from the inspector is that we have manufactured about 20 per cent of mixed manilla, but that the greater part, 80 per cent of it, is pure manilla, the intention being to satisfy a demand for that sort of twine which the inspector says exists. It seems to me that my hon. friend will be able to judge, when I gave the figures at which we sold, whether we ought at these figures to have been able to dispose of this twine. He has had more experience with this matter than I have. My impression is that these figures were lower than the market prices ruling at the time.

Referring to the matter brought up by the hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Lefurgey) as to the quality of the twine, I may say that in going among the farmers-and I think that other members here have met with the same experience-I find there is throughout the country a prejudice against the twine that is manufactured at Kingston. There is only a limited amount made there and consumed in the country, and when I ask farmers why they do not buy Kingston twine they tell me that the American twine is far better. It is unfortunate that we have not in this country a sufficiently strong Canadian sentiment to enable us successfully to put upon the market an article such as the twine to which we are now referring. I have heard the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) within the last two years express, similar views, and regret the fact that Canadian sentiment did not uphold Canadian products. Our people buy things because they are foreign. I will venture to say that 75 per cent of the farmers of this country will buy American twine because it is American. They have an impression that because it comes from the .other side it is better, and the government of the day is largely responsible for this lack of Canadian sentiment. The whole policy of the present government is to cultivate a sentiment amongst the people of this country in favour of purchasing goods that are produced in other countries, and to lessen the' purchase of Canadian goods. I attribute very largely the feeling that the penitentiary binder twine is inferior just to this lack of Canadian sentiment. People are -willing to buy American twine because it comes from the other side on the principle that far away fields are green, and it is felt that if it is only brought from some other country it must of necessity be better. In the section of country in which I live a large amount of American twine is used. They use chiefly what is known as Plymouth. I asked one man : Why do you buy this Plymouth, and he said :	It is so
much better. Farmers will not use the penitentiary twine. For anything I know it is equal in all respects to the imported

twine and quite possible this very twine that is bought by our farmers as American twine ig Canadian twine. I do not doubt that in many instances that it is a fact, because our Canadian factories are making twine, shipping- it across to the United States and selling it to the very men who supply twine to dealers in this country, and I have no doubt that it goes there, comes back here as American twine and takes the market much better, selling as American twine in competition with the Kingston article, although it is of purely Canadian manufacture. It is as I said the lack of a good Canadian sentiment that interferes very materially with the reputation and sale of the Kingston twine.
I am sorry for Halton.

The government today by their whole policy of preferential tariff and free trade in twine, &c., are cultivating that lack of sentiment, and until some change is made in the policy of the government I am afraid these difficulties will crop up from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would like the hon. member to tell me how to cultivate that sentiment which will induce farmers to purchase our twine. I think my hon. friend ought to cultivate the sentiment in his own constituency, and instead of making that fine speech, which is addressed exclusively to me, if he would go to his own constituency and tell his electors what they ought to do in the premises,' he would be rendering a great service, and I am quite sure we will all appreciate his efforts.

Yes, I have been (endeavouring to do that all along the line, but I confess that when I have the whole force and policy of the government against me I find great difficulty and what I complain of is that the government will not change their policy. If the government would join me in the principles I advocate, we could very soon change that sentiment for the better interest of the country and of the Kingston binder twine manufactory. I would like the Minister of Justice to join me in advocating a better Canadian sentiment and to shape the policy of the government along lines that will invite people to use Canadian goods, Canadian cottons, Canadian woollens, binder twine, binders and everything that you can think of, Canadian. Let us cultivate a purely Canadian sentiment. If you go to the United States and enter a shop you will see that if a piece of cotton is laid on the counter, probably ninety-nine out of one hundred ladies will buy that piece of American cotton because it is American. Will the Minister of Justice undertake to say that there ts the same sentiment among our Canadian people? It is a matter of extreme regret to me and we must adopt some policy in this
country that will produce a better Canadian sentiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: * I am not in woollens or cottons or ladies furnishings ; I 'am in binder twine and if my hon. friend will undertake to tell me how I can sell my binder twine I shall be very glad. I cannot deal with vague generalities about Canadian sentiment; I have to get back to binder twine. If he will help me to sell my binder twine I will be satisfied.
Just create the sentiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And the taste for ladies furnishings.

Give the Canadian market a taste for twine made in Canada, impose such protection as will preserve our market for Canadian twine, and inside of five years you will have such a strong sentiment in favour of Canadian twine that I undertake to say there will be no question about the quality of the twine you produce.

On the question of Kingston twine I wish to express my opinion. I think that the twine manufactured there is good and the farmers of this country have no ground of complaint whatever. The twine coming into my own county is generally appreciated by people of both political parties, if you -wish to discuss the-matter from a political standpoint. But what I say is that there must be something wrong in the department somewhere if the twine is not sold. I do not wish to complain- jjerhaps 1 would not be in a position to point out where the changes should be- but I think that if the Kingston penitentiary is manufacturing good twine, as in my' opinion it is, the situation would be improved by manufacturing only pure manilla twine, abandoning the manufacture of the other kind altogether. Then I think that parliament would endorse the minister in spending some money to ensure the sale of the twine direct to the farmer. There must be something at fault in the department somewhere or this quantity of twine which is very small in proportion to the quantity used, would be sold every year. In view of the fact 1hat an enormous quantity of twine is used in Canada, there is something wrong somewhere, or else the twine would be sold every year. I may say that in my own county a great many orders have been sent in during the last three years, and they have not been supplied, for the reason that the department stated that they were sold out of pure manilla twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite right -the G50 feet twine.
A few counties would consume every pound of twine almost, manufactured in the Kingston penitentiary, but my hon. friend is not manufacturing the kind the farmers want.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Might I ask what has been done in reference to the claims that were made against the government on account of poor twine ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The inspector tells me that every claim that has been put in has been satisfactorily adjusted, and that there is not a single claim now pending.
I understood from the parties who spoke to me a few months ago that the claim that they had put in had not at that time been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give me the name of the party ?
Mr. Lee, of Victoria.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon friend will send us a note we will look into it. i want to say there is a prejudice all over this country against prison-made goods, and that prejudice applies to binder twine and operates to the detriment of the factory. It is a prejudice that is fostered in some directions probably by the labour unions. Of course, we think that our twine is good. I am so advised at all events, and I see no reason why in the interest of Canada at large, our twine should not be bought. After all, this is the people's factory ; the people of Canada are flaying for this. It is an attempt honestly made by the government to protect the farmers of Canada against the combine outside; and even if it does cost a little to keep it going, it seems to me that the people of the country ought to appreciate the fact that we are making this effort.

The hon. minister has told us that this is an effort to protect the farmers. I would like him to tell me how he is going to protect the farmers by putting his twine on the market at a price just a shade below the price fixed by the great American trust. It is well known that the cost of twine is not what fixes the price; it is just what the great American trust chooses to fix it at ; and yet the minister fixes his price just. within a shade of the combine price. Under these circumstances, I do not think that he is offering much protection to the farmer. The way to fix the price would be upon the basis of the actual cost of the material and labour. I believe the best twine made in the country is not pure manilla. I do not think the farmers want pure manilla. They want a twine composed of about 60 per cent manilla and 40 per cent sisal. The quantity of pure manilla twine used in this country is quite small as compared with the mixed twine. If you take 60 per cent of the cost of a pound of manilla fibre and 40 per cent of the cost of a pound of sisal, and remember that about 20 per cent of the whole Mr. BLAIN.
thing is coarse oil, a cheaper article, you will bring the cost of the binder twine very much below the figure which the minister gives. That would be the true way to fix the price if you wanted to protect the farmer, and not simply to shade below the price of the combine.

There is a good deal of (his twine sold in my section of the country; but the farmers got a bad impression of it because at first they could not get the twine they wanted, and later on it was sold to a private dealer for about half the money they paid. For instance, the farmer paid 10c a pound and the private dealer bought the balance for 5c, and the impression got abroad that the department were selling at too high a price to the farmer, and were losing on what was sold to the private dealer. With regard to the price, it is generally conceded that whatever the raw material costs, binder twine can be made at a fair profit for about lc a pound ; so that if the raw material cost an average of Sic. a pound, the government could sell it at 94c and have a fair profit. I would suggest that if the government would allow a small commission to some person to go around among the farmers and take orders, they would sell a very much larger quantity of twine. The complaint of parties who took orders in my section was that they practically got nothing in the shape of a commission that would be a fair compensation for their labour, or they could have sold a great deal more of it. That might be done for the benefit of both the department and the farmers.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: I move that the House do now adjourn. My hon. friend yesterday asked me for some information in regard to the Transportation Commission. The Commission to-day is composed of Mr. Robert Reford, of Montreal ; Mr. Edward C. Fry, of Quebec, and Mr. J. H. Ashdown, of Winnipeg. It has not made a report. I think it made an interim report last year in regard to St. John. Mr. Reford, I am sorry to say, has tendered his resignation on account of illness. We have asked him to reconsider his determination, and have not heard from him since.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?
The resolution of the Minister of Justice with regard to the appointment of judges to the Railway Commission, then the Census Bill, and then Supply, taking up the Public Works estimates.
